extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in journalism and historical scholarship; journalists, historians, and those concerned with plagiarism standards
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate whether borrowing from sources in historical or journalistic prose constitutes plagiarism, using academic styleguide and professional-historical-association standards as the benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadvertent copying counts as plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Unintentional or 'inadvertent' copying is treated as plagiarism by major style and professional bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MLA Handbook devotes a section to 'unintentional plagiarism' and explains it 'sometimes happens because researchers do not keep precise records of their reading, and by the time they return to their notes, they have forgotten whether their summaries and paraphrases contain quoted material that is poorly marked or unmarked.' The American Historical Association's statement rejects an exemption based on intent and treats the 'misled by hastily taken and imperfect notes' defense as evidence of shoddy work rather than an exculpatory factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent is not required; negligence suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism standards do not rely solely on deliberate intent to deceive; negligence or failure to follow proper practices can constitute plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the AHA prior to 1990 included 'with an intent to deceive' in its definition, contemporary guidance (MLA, AHA, Harvard practices) treats negligence—e.g., poor note-taking or failure to check drafts against sources—as sufficient to establish plagiarism. As historian Stanley Kutler is quoted: 'intent alone does not make plagiarism. Negligence, whether purposeful or inadvertent, does just fine.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenting exact wording without quotation marks is plagiarism even if cited
rubrics_metrics.description: Using an author's exact wording without marking it as a quotation is plagiarism, even when the source is cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MLA Guide: 'Presenting an author’s exact wording without marking it as a quotation is plagiarism, even if you cite the source.' Thus proper quoting (quotation marks or block quotation format) is required when reproducing exact phrasing; citation alone is not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended borrowing can be plagiarism even with attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: An extended borrowing of another author's distinctive material can constitute plagiarism even if the source is acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AHA/OAH: 'Plagiarism also includes the limited borrowing, without attribution, of another person’s distinctive and significant research findings, hypotheses, theories, rhetorical strategies, or interpretations, or an extended borrowing even with attribution.' The implication is that quantity, distinctiveness, and closeness of borrowing matter; attribution does not automatically authorize extensive reuse of another's prose or structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrase that follows source too closely is plagiarism even if cited
rubrics_metrics.description: If a writer's sentences follow the source closely in idea and sentence structure so they are 'closer to quotation than to paraphrase,' that is plagiarism despite citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harvard guidance: 'If your own sentences follow the source so closely in idea and sentence structure that the result is really closer to quotation than to paraphrase ... you are plagiarizing, even if you have cited the source.' Proper paraphrase requires genuine rephrasing and reworking of ideas, not near-verbatim retention of structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must check manuscripts against underlying texts prior to publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars are obliged to verify their drafts against original sources to prevent inadvertent borrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AHA's statement counsels that the defense of imperfect notes 'will be easily disposed of if scholars take seriously the injunction to check their manuscripts against the underlying texts prior to publication.' This functions as a procedural requirement and a quality-control criterion: diligent checking reduces the risk of plagiarism findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to disclose, hide evidence, or delay corrections undermines integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Concealing evidence of borrowing, failing to disclose discovered problems, or leaving plagiarized passages in later editions damages an author's claim to high moral or professional standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticizes behavior such as hiding evidence, not acknowledging borrowings until exposed by press, and leaving plagiarized portions intact in subsequent editions. Such conduct is presented as ethically problematic and relevant to judgments about character and professional integrity.
